title: Fair Isle scarf
subtitle: A flat scarf with a repeating two-colour Fair Isle yoke pattern.
excerpt: A scarf knitted flat in two-colour stranded colourwork on 3.5 mm needles with fingering-weight yarn, finishing at 18 cm wide by 160 cm long. The main body is stocking stitch in a single colour with six Fair Isle pattern bands of 25 rows each, worked from a 10-stitch by 25-row chart. Each pattern band uses a contrast colour against the main colour.
sourceNotes: Fair Isle stranded colourwork patterns with repeating geometric motifs are documented in traditional Shetland knitting from the early 19th century, with museum examples at the Shetland Museum. Mary Thomas's Knitting Book (1938) documents the two-colour stranding technique, citations only. The specific chart here is original.

glossaryTerms.definition: A technique in which two yarn colours are carried across every row. The yarn not currently in use is stranded (floated) across the wrong side of the work.
A style of stranded two-colour colourwork originating in Shetland, characterised by geometric patterns in repeating bands and a maximum float span of about five stitches.
A cast-on forming a neat elastic edge by using the tail and working yarn over two fingers simultaneously.

content.text: This is a flat scarf knitted in two-colour
Fair Isle
stranded colourwork

on 3.5 mm needles with fingering-weight yarn, finishing at 18 cm wide and 160 cm long when blocked. The scarf has six pattern bands worked from a 10-stitch by 25-row chart, spaced along the length with plain stocking stitch in the main colour between each band. Within each band both yarns are carried across every row; the yarn not in use is floated across the wrong side.

Flat construction was chosen over in-the-round because the wrong side is occasionally visible on a worn scarf. A flat fabric has neater floats on the wrong side when worked carefully. Managing a float on a purl row (wrong side) is the main skill challenge of this pattern.
What you need

items.name: Fingering-weight yarn, main colour (MC)
items.substitutions: Any fingering-weight yarn. Smooth yarn makes colour changes more visible.

items.name: Fingering-weight yarn, contrast colour (CC)
items.substitutions: Strong contrast against MC for clearest pattern definition.

items.name: 3.5 mm needles, straight or circular (UK 9.5 / US 4)

content.text: Gauge

28 sts x 36 rows = 10 x 10 cm in stocking stitch on 3.5 mm needles, blocked. Stranded colourwork typically knits at the same or very slightly tighter gauge than plain stocking stitch, so swatch in the chart pattern. One stitch per 10 cm off gauge shifts the finished width by about 0.6 cm at this stitch count. Blocking is essential for colourwork: the finished scarf grows approximately 5 to 8 percent in width and the floats relax completely with blocking.
Stitches used

K (knit), P (purl). Stocking stitch flat: K on RS, P on WS. In pattern rows, always keep the non-working yarn at the back (away from you) on RS rows and at the front (toward you) on WS rows so the floats sit consistently on the same side of the fabric. Never twist the two yarns around each other during a colour change unless specifically catching a float.
Reading the chart

Read RS rows from right to left, WS rows from left to right. The chart is 10 stitches wide. With 50 stitches on the needle, work the 10-stitch repeat 5 times across. The 25-row chart constitutes one full pattern band. Work six pattern bands total, with approximately 16 rows of plain MC stocking stitch between each band, and 20 rows of plain stocking stitch at each end.
Pattern
Cast on
Use the
long-tail cast-on

in MC to place 50 stitches on the needle. The stitch count is a multiple of 10 for the chart repeat. Before beginning, calculate the tail: tail_cm = (needle circumference mm x stitch count) / 10 + 15. For 3.5 mm needles (circumference approximately 11 mm) and 50 stitches: (11 x 50) / 10 + 15 = 55 + 15 = 70 cm. Leave at least 70 cm of MC tail.
Stitch count check-in: after the cast-on you should have 50 stitches on the needle.
Body
Cast-on edge (20 rows): work in MC stocking stitch.

Pattern band 1 (25 rows): join CC at the right edge on a RS row. Work chart rows 1 to 25, carrying both yarns and working the 10-stitch repeat 5 times across. Drop CC at the end of row 25; do not cut unless changing colourway between bands.
Separator (16 rows): work in MC stocking stitch.
Repeat [pattern band (25 rows) + separator (16 rows)] 4 more times. Then work pattern band 6 (25 rows). End with 20 rows of plain MC stocking stitch.
Stitch count check-in: at the halfway mark (approximately row 288 of the full body) you should have 50 stitches on the needle.
Bind off
Work a standard bind-off in MC on a RS row. Tension the bind-off to match the cast-on edge.
Common faults

Colourwork puckering. The most common cause is floats worked too tightly. Before working each float, spread the stitches on the right needle so the float spans the full stretched width rather than the relaxed width. Practice on the first pattern band before the fabric is too long to adjust.

WS purl rows tighter than RS knit rows. Many knitters automatically purl more tightly than they knit. If the pattern bands look tighter on alternate rows, try purling with the needle held slightly further out or switch to a needle one size larger for the WS rows of the pattern bands.

Floats tangling at the right edge when re-joining CC at each pattern band. When re-joining CC, work the first two stitches holding both yarns together, then proceed with the chart. This catches the CC tail without a separate weaving-in step.
Finishing

Weave in all MC and CC tails on the wrong side, following the float direction. Block thoroughly: soak for 20 minutes in cool water, press out water gently, lay flat on blocking mats and pin to 18 x 160 cm. Allow to dry completely before unpinning.
Care
Handwash in cool water with wool wash. Do not rub or wring. Lay flat to dry. Reblock if the pattern bands contract after washing.
What to try next

The mosaic colourwork scarf achieves a similar graphic look without floating: mosaic knitting slips stitches rather than carrying both yarns on the same row. The Bohus-inspired mini scarf uses a small colourwork yoke on a short neckwarmer length, which is a quicker project in the same technique.
